How much more so, since Allah the Mighty sent down in her innocence the explicit words of His eternal speech, and enclosed her, from its beginning to its end, with these two verses that point to the customary proof.

A mention of the hadith "Souls are armies mobilised" and what accords with it was made earlier at the verse ﴿The fornicator﴾ [al-Nur: 3], but it did not comprehensively cite its takhrij (sourcing). It was recorded by Muslim in the Book of Adab of his Sahih, and by Abu Dawud in his Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Souls are armies mobilised. Those among them that recognise one another are harmonious, and those among them that are strangers to one another are at odds." And in another narration from him, traced to the Prophet: "People are mines like the mines of gold and silver. The best of them in the Jahiliyya are the best of them in Islam, when they have understanding. And souls are armies mobilised. Those among them that recognise one another are harmonious, and those among them that are strangers to one another are at odds." This hadith is also narrated from ʿĀʾisha the Mother of the Believers, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Salman al-Farisi, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, and ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasa, may Allah be pleased with them all. Al-Bukhari included the hadith of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, in his Sahih in a form of definitive attribution (ta'liq), and connected it (wasala) in al-Adab al-Mufrad; likewise al-Isma'ili in al-Mustakhraj, and Abu al-Shaykh in the Book of Proverbs (Kitab al-Amthal). Its attribution to Abu Yaʿla was mentioned earlier. The wording of the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is: "What was for Allah became harmonious, and what was for other than Allah became at odds." Abu al-Shaykh recorded it in al-Amthal. The wording of the hadith of Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, is: "When they meet, they sniff one another as horses sniff, and those that recognise one another are harmonious..." — the hadith.

As for the hadith of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat in the biography of Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Saqti, and Abu ʿAbd Allah ibn Mandah in Kitab al-Ruh, from Salim ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, from his father, who said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: 'O Abu al-Hasan! Sometimes you were present while we were absent, and sometimes we were present while you were absent. Three things I want to ask you about: do you have knowledge of any of them? A man loves a man yet has not seen good from him, and a man hates a man yet has not seen evil from him.' ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Yes! I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the souls are armies mobilised. Those among them that recognise one another are harmonious, and those among them that are strangers to one another are at odds."' ʿUmar said: 'One.' He said: 'And a man narrates a hadith, then forgets it, [and while he is with it and has forgotten it,] then he remembers it?' ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Among hearts there is no heart but that it has a cloud like the cloud over the moon. While the moon is shining, a cloud covers it and it becomes dark; then when it clears, it shines. Likewise, while the heart is speaking, a cloud envelops it and it forgets; then when it clears from it, it remembers."' ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Two.' He said: 'And a man sees a dream: some of it comes true and some of it is false?' He said: 'Yes! I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No servant or handmaid sleeps and falls into deep sleep but that his soul is raised up to the Throne. The one that does not awaken except at the Throne, that is the dream that comes true; and the one that awakens short of the Throne, that is the dream that is false."' ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Three things I was seeking, and praise be to Allah who let me attain them before death.'"

Likewise al-Tabarani recorded the hadith of Salman, like the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with them all. They also recited, on the same theme, lines by Abu Nuwas:

*Indeed the hearts are mobilised armies,*
*for Allah on earth, recognising one another by their desires.*

*Whatever among them recognises another is harmonious,*
*and whatever among them is strange to another is at odds.*

Since this has been established, its conclusion is certain: ﴿Those﴾, that is, those characterised by purity and goodness in the highest degree, ﴿are cleared﴾ by the clearing of Allah and the clearing of everyone who reflects on such proof, ﴿of what they say﴾, that is, of the slanderers, the vilest of people, because she would not be the wife of the best of the good unless she herself were like that.

Since He established their innocence, He began anew the report of their reward, and said: ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, that is, for whatever shortcoming they may have committed, if they committed any. And since this was in the context of urging spending upon some of the slanderers, He said: ﴿And a generous provision﴾, that is, they live by it a good life, and they treat well those who wronged them, and this does not diminish it, given its generosity in itself, with its abundance, its goodness, and other qualities of generosity.

When He, glorified is He, had concluded the matter of the innocence of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, in this manner, by which He clothed her in such honour and adorned her with such virtues of excellence and splendour, and as though the people of the slander had, by their slander, opened the door to evil suspicions out of enmity from Iblīs toward the people of this religion, after they had been, in that and in much of their dispositions, upon the first natural disposition (fiṭra), being content among them with the disease of polytheism (shirk), He, exalted is He, commanded, in refutation of what Satan had stirred up by his whisperings of disease, to keep away from the places of accusation and from being involved in anything that cuts off corruption. So He said: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, that is, bind yourselves to this religion, ﴿do not enter﴾, any one of you, and perhaps He addressed the group (p-٢٤٩) because they were likely to drive away Satan by some of them adorning themselves in the presence of others with the garment of piety. Whoever among them fell short, his brothers would restrain him, and so Satan would not be able to gain power over him. Therefore the prohibition addressed to the one falls under the same ruling a fortiori. ﴿houses other than your houses﴾, that is, those which are your dwellings, ﴿until you seek permission﴾, that is, you ask, by seeking permission, that those within them become familiar with you and you become familiar with them. For if it were said to him, "Who is it?" and he said, "I," familiarity would not be achieved, because of their not knowing him. Rather, what he must do is say, "I am so-and-so," naming himself by that by which he is known, so that he may be made familiar, and thus he is permitted to enter, or else is disliked and turned away. ﴿and greet its people﴾, that is, those who are its inhabitants, even if by means of those who are lent to you, so that you say, "Peace be upon you! May I enter?" or knock upon the door, if it may be that they do not hear the request for permission, so that they may give you leave. ﴿That﴾, the exalted matter which I have commanded you, ﴿is better for you﴾ than what you used to do of entering without permission and of the greeting of the Jāhiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance). For when you enter without permission, you may often see what displeases you, but when you ask permission, you will not enter upon what you dislike. This is in this world, and as for the Hereafter, it is greater. Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, may Allah be pleased with him, has related: "If one gives the greeting three times and no one answers him, let him return." (p-٢٥٠)

This applies when he thinks that the householder has heard.

Since every person is never free of states which he dislikes to be exposed or interrupted, He said: ﴿so that you may remember﴾, that is, so that your state may be that of one who is hoped to remember, by returning to himself upon hearing this prohibition, and so he knows that what displeases him from others displeases others from him, and so he does toward them what he loves to be done toward him, out of fear of reciprocation, for recompense is of the same kind as the deed. And whatever is obligatory upon him outside his house is recommended for him inside his house, such as clearing the throat and raising the voice with mention (of Allah) and the like, as the hadith prohibiting knocking at night indicates, so that he does not see from his family what he dislikes.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 28:

Since the occupants may be absent, and a person, being a private matter (ʿawrah), does not like to let others see all his affairs, He said: ﴿And if you find no one in them﴾, that is, in the houses in which you have no residence, ﴿anyone﴾ who might forbid you, then Allah forbids you from them, giving precedence to the averting of harms (dar' al-mafasid), ﴿then do not enter them﴾, that is, ever, ﴿until permission is given to you﴾ by one who gives permission, whether by lawful permission from the occupant or from another, because entering is a disposal of another's property or right, so it is not lawful without his permission. And since it was as if it were said: "If you are permitted in something you have not asked permission for, then enter," He followed it with His saying: ﴿And if it is said to you﴾ by a speaker, namely when you ask permission to enter a house and it is empty or someone is in it: ﴿Go back, then go back﴾, that is, and do not be too proud to be confronted with what you dislike, such as a plain refusal, for the truth is more deserving of being followed, and people have private matters and affairs which they do not like others to see.

Since in refusal there is a deficiency that causes humiliation and constriction in the breast, He, glorified is He, promised in return something that compensates for that, so He said, by way of resumption: ﴿That﴾, that is, this specific returning, ﴿is purer﴾, that is, more pure and more growing, ﴿for you﴾, for in it there is purity from the humiliation of standing at the door of another, and growth through what comes to the owner of the house of shame when his command to return is obeyed, along with what there is in that before Allah.

Since the implied meaning is: "Allah rewards you for obeying His command," and since a person may do, in empty houses and others, hidden matters that contradict what He, glorified is He, has taught, which appear to be a benefit but are in fact a harm, He followed that implied clause with His saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King. Since the intended meaning is emphasis on knowledge, He placed the prepositional phrase first, so that it becomes as when you ask a person about the knowledge of something and he says to you: "I know no one else," and then he says: ﴿knows what you do﴾, that is, even if its matter is obscure to the most astute of creatures, ﴿All-Knowing﴾, nothing of it is hidden from Him, however subtle it may be. So beware of dubious matters: when you stand to ask permission, do not stand directly facing the door, but to its right or its left, because asking permission was only prescribed for the sake of sight, and avoid looking into the openings through which one of the people of the house may look to know who is at the door: is it someone with whom he is comfortable, so that he is admitted, or not, so that he is turned away. And similar to this are its like, matters not hidden from a discerning, God-fearing person, whose thought soars over the wide range of what it indicates, such as the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "When a man speaks and then turns, it is a trust." Narrated by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 29:

When some places are ones in which no one may be found to whom entry is permitted, either because they are empty or because the one who lodges there does not have exclusive rights to them, such as caravanserais (*khanat*) and hostels (*ribat*), he followed what preceded with a clarification that such places are not included in the prohibition. So he said, resuming the discourse: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, meaning no inclination with blame at all, ﴿to enter houses﴾ such as the caravanserais and hostels, ﴿uninhabited﴾. Then he described them by his saying: ﴿in which there is provision﴾ (p-٢٥٣), meaning enjoyment through some kind of benefit, such as seeking shade and the like, ﴿for you﴾. This includes what is prepared for the guest, if its owner gave permission for it at the outset and the guest placed his belongings in it, because seeking permission (*istidhan*) is so that one does not burst in upon what one wishes to keep hidden and wishes to keep concealed from the knowledge of others. So when that is not feared, there is no point to seeking permission.

Since the implied meaning was: "Then God does not withhold from you what benefits you, and does not harm others," he joined to it his saying: ﴿And God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿knows﴾ at every moment ﴿what you disclose﴾. He emphasized this by repeating the relative pronoun, so he said: ﴿and what you conceal﴾, as a warning against crowding out anyone in what is permissible in a way that harms him and constricts him, while using the basis of permission as a pretext, or being admitted to a dwelling and concealing treachery within it. For even if one guards against betrayers by means of the veil, mixing with people is unavoidable, because man is built with a need for companionship. For this reason, the following statement of His, exalted is He, was connected to it by way of resumption, addressing the most exalted of His creation in understanding and the most precise of them in preserving His command, to the exclusion of the rest, as an indication of the difficulty of the matter and the gravity of the situation, warning them of turning away from them by clothing oneself in the garment of pride and veiling oneself in a position of dominance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 30:

﴿Say to the believing men﴾. He used the descriptive term (lil-mu'minin, "to the believers") as a sign that after mingling (with women) one is not able to guard against being exposed to them, and that only one whose faith has taken firm root in his heart will restrain himself in such a situation, because the betrayal (of the eye) is then hidden. This is unlike what preceded regarding the prohibition of entering (others' homes), where the expression used was "those who believe" (alladhina amanu). ﴿Lower﴾ (yaghuddu) means they should lower (their gaze) and not raise it, but rather refrain from what they have been forbidden.

Since the matter is extremely difficult, He said ﴿from their gazes﴾ (min absarihim), with the partitive "min" (tab'idiyya, "some of") affirmed, as a sign that the first glance is pardoned, and that what is held against a person is only persistence (in looking). And since the gaze is the messenger of fornication, He placed it first.

Since guarding the private parts (hifz al-farj) is easier than guarding the gaze, because the danger of intercourse is more serious and because one does not do it without deliberate testing, He omitted "min" to intend generality, and said ﴿and guard their private parts﴾, meaning from every prohibited thing, including exposure and other things. He did not make an exception for a wife or what the right hand possesses, relying on what preceded in (Surat) al-Mu'minun. Also, the context is one of emphasis on the seriousness of the matter of guarding and of strictness. He encouraged this by giving its reason in His saying ﴿That﴾, i.e., this lofty, great matter of both lowering (the gaze) and guarding, which I have commanded them, ﴿is purer for them﴾, meaning it is closer to their growing, increasing and being purified physically and spiritually, and to their being blessed. As for the physical (purification), fornication brings death by plague and causes poverty and other calamities. "No people among whom fornication appears, but they are seized by famine."

Narrated by Ahmad from 'Amr ibn al-'As (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also narrated from him by Abu'l-Qasim 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd al-Hakam in the Kitab al-Futuh, and its wording is: "No people among whom fornication appears, but they are seized by annihilation (al-fana), and no people among whom usury appears, but they are seized by famine (al-sanah), and no people among whom bribery appears, but they are seized by terror (al-ru'b). Fornication brings poverty." Narrated by al-Bayhaqi from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), and when fornication appears, poverty and destitution appear. Narrated by Ibn Majah and al-Bazzar, and this is his wording, from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both); and al-Bayhaqi, whose wording is: "Fornication brings poverty." In another narration of his: "Never has indecency appeared among a people and been practised openly among them, but plague and diseases unknown to their predecessors have appeared among them." It was also narrated from him by Ibn Ishaq in the Sirah, in the account of the expedition of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf (may Allah be pleased with him) to Dumat al-Jandal, and its wording is: "Indeed, indecency has never appeared among a people until they proclaim it, but there has appeared among them plague and diseases that were not in their forefathers who passed away. And they did not diminish the measure and the scale, but they were seized by years of drought, hardship of sustenance and the tyranny of rulers. And they did not withhold zakat from their wealth, but they were withheld rain from the sky; were it not for the animals, they would not be given rain. And they did not break the covenant of Allah and His Messenger, but Allah set over them an enemy from other than themselves, who took some of what was in their hands. And whenever their leaders do not rule by the Book of Allah and act tyrannically in what Allah has revealed, Allah makes their violence fall upon one another." In al-Targhib by al-Mundhiri, from Ibn Majah, al-Bazzar and al-Bayhaqi, from him (may Allah be pleased with him), something similar to this wording is narrated. And at the end of the Sirah, from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) in his sermon when he assumed the caliphate: "No people abandon jihad in the way of Allah but Allah strikes them with humiliation, and fornication never spreads among a people but Allah sends affliction upon them all."

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, that it reached him from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "Embezzlement never appears among a people but Allah casts terror into their hearts; fornication never spreads among a people but death becomes abundant among them; a people never diminish the measure and the scale but Allah cuts off their provision from them; a people never judge by other than the truth but bloodshed spreads among them; and a people never break a covenant but Allah sets over them the enemy."

Al-Tabarani narrated in al-Awsat, from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When fornication increases, corruption increases, and the ruler becomes tyrannical." And in it: "I liken them in that age to the compromiser. When usury and fornication appear in a town, Allah permits its destruction." Narrated by al-Tabarani from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both).

As for the spiritual (purification), Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Umamah (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "No Muslim looks at the beauty of a woman and then lowers his gaze, but Allah replaces for him an act of worship, the sweetness of which he finds."

Ibn Kathir said: This has also been narrated as a marfu' report from Ibn 'Umar, Hudhayfah and 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with them), but there is weakness in their chains. He cited as a supporting report from al-Tabarani, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "Indeed, the glance is one of the poisoned arrows of Iblis. Whoever leaves it out of fear of Me, I will replace it for him with faith, the sweetness of which he finds in his heart." From this it is known that whoever adorns himself with what Allah has commanded here, his heart becomes a place for wisdom, his action is worthy of success, and his mention is joined with acceptance.

Since zaka' includes increase and purification, and since the discussion here is about lowering the gaze, and since purity is very evident in it, there was no need for a call to emphasis by explicitly stating purity. As for the verse of al-Baqarah, since it concerned preventing (a woman from remarriage, 'adl), and this happens only out of grudges and enmities, the guardian might think that withholding her from the one who prevents her is purer for him and for her. So (Allah) reinforced the expression with the verb of zaka' by explicitly stating what was understood from purity.

Since the situation is difficult because souls incline toward lowly things and follow their desires, He gave the reason for this command, encouraging and warning, by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., He to whom nothing is hidden, by virtue of His complete encompassing knowledge, ﴿is All-Aware﴾. Since the restraint of modesty, along with that, is a great obstacle, one does not transgress it except through treatment and training, He expressed it with (the word) "doing" (sana'a), saying ﴿of what they do﴾, i.e., even if they go to great lengths to conceal it and scrutinize the planning of their deception in it.

[p. 259] When He began with the men who are the qawwamah (protectors and maintainers) over women, He followed with the women, saying: ﴿And say to the believing women...﴾. He likewise encouraged them through this noble attribute, ﴿that they lower their gaze﴾. Since what is intended is lowering the gaze from some of the things seen, namely the mahram (those who are unmarriageable to them), He said: ﴿from their gaze﴾. So they should not follow up their glance with a look at what is forbidden, whether a man or anything else. As for the report from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, concerning looking at the Abyssinians' games in the mosque, the scholars answered it by suggesting that she was below the age of puberty, because she said: "Estimate the measure of a young girl, of tender age, eager for play."

﴿And that they guard their private parts﴾ from what is not lawful for them, such as exposure and other things. Since women are the snares of Satan, they were commanded to increase their covering, through His saying [p. 259] prohibiting adornment, so that the prohibition against the places of adornment on the body would be stronger and more fitting: ﴿And that they not display their adornment﴾, i.e., such as jewelry and fine garments, so how much more so what lies beyond these. ﴿Except what appears of it﴾, i.e., what is of such a nature that it appears and it would be difficult to guard against revealing it, so it shows without intent, such as the bracelet, the ring, and kohl, for a woman must necessarily handle her needs with her hands, and uncover her face in testimony and the like.

Since most adornment is on the necks, hands, and feet, and it is easier and more feasible to keep the necks constantly covered, He singled them out and said: ﴿And let them draw down﴾. Ḍaraba (to strike, to draw) means placing something quickly and with force. It is said: "daraba fī 'amalihi" (he set about his work); "daraba bi-yadihi ilā kadhā" (he swung his hand toward such-and-such); "daraba 'alā yadihi" (he held on to his hand); "daraba al-layl bi-awrāqihi" (the night came with its leaves, i.e., it advanced); al-ḍārib: the night whose darkness has spread to the right and left and filled the world; and al-ḍārib: the tall one of anything, and the moving one.

Since what is intended by this drawing down is a portion of the khimār, namely that part of it that adheres to the neckline, He used the preposition bi- with it and said: ﴿with their khumur﴾, the plural of khimār, which is a kerchief placed over the head. Abu Hayyan said: it is the veil that a woman casts over her head.

﴿over their juyub﴾, the plural of jayb, which is the opening of the garment that [p. 260] surrounds the neck. The meaning then is that they should bring it down over what lies beneath the neck, letting it hang on all sides, and lengthening it to cover the hair, the chest, and other parts there. It seems the word ḍarb was chosen to indicate the strength of intention for covering, and to indicate forgiveness for what may appear when the khimār moves during some activity. Abu Hayyan said: The women used to cover their heads with khumur and let them fall down behind the backs, so the throat, the neck, and the ears remained uncovered.

Al-Bukhari reported in the Tafsir, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "May Allah have mercy on the first emigrant women. When the verse ﴿and let them draw down their khumur over their juyub﴾ was revealed, they split their murut (cloaks) — and in another version, they took their izar (wrappers) and tore them along the edges — and covered themselves with them." That is, they concealed what was in front. The izar here means the milhaf (wrap).

Since mention of the jayb might lead one to think it is specifically about adornment, He generalized with His saying: ﴿And that they not display﴾, or repeated it to clarify to whom display is permitted and to whom it is not, and for emphasis: ﴿their adornment﴾, i.e., the hidden adornment, wherever it may be, on the neck or elsewhere, [p. 261] apart from the face, the two palms, and the appearance of the two feet, by wearing the jilbab, which is the garment that covers the clothes, and the khimar. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

﴿except to their husbands (bu'ulah)﴾, i.e., their husbands, for adornment was made for them. Abu Hayyan said: Then He mentioned the mahrams and treated them equally regarding display of adornment, but their ranks in prohibition differ according to what is in human souls; the father and the brother are not like the husband's son. End of quote. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿or their fathers﴾, i.e., for they have over them the compassion that prevents looking with desire. Similarly in this sense are paternal and maternal uncles, and each of them is called a father metaphorically, as in His saying: ﴿the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. ﴿or the fathers of their husbands﴾, for their mercy toward their children is a barrier. ﴿or their sons﴾, for they have over them the awe that keeps away such things. ﴿or the sons of their husbands﴾, for the awe of their fathers is a barrier. ﴿or their brothers﴾, for they have, out of desire to protect them from shame, what guards against suspicion. ﴿or the sons of﴾ — He turned away from the broken plural to avoid four pronouns in a row without a strong separator, which would diminish its smoothness — ﴿their brothers, or the sons of their sisters﴾, for they are like their sons. ﴿or their women﴾, i.e., Muslim women. As for non-Muslim women, their ruling is the ruling of men. [p. 262] Sa'id ibn Mansur reported in his Sunan from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he wrote to 'Ubayda, may Allah be pleased with him, forbidding the dhimmi women from entering the bathhouse with Muslim women, and said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day that anyone should look at her nakedness except the people of her religion." And in the Musnad of 'Abd ibn Humayd there is something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

﴿or what their right hands possess﴾, i.e., of males and females, even if they are not Muslims, because of the awe they have over them. Ibn al-Musayyib restricted the verse to female slaves only. Abu Hayyan said: al-Zamakhshari said: "This is the correct view, because a woman's male slave is in the position of a non-mahram stranger to her, whether he is a eunuch or a fully male." It is reported from Maysun bint Bahdal al-Kalbiyya that Mu'awiya, may Allah be pleased with him, entered upon her with a eunuch, and she covered herself from him. He said: "He is a eunuch." She said: "O Mu'awiya! Do you think that mutilating him makes lawful what Allah has forbidden?" End of quote.

The story of Mabur refutes this. As for his saying "al-Kilabiyya," our shaykh said in his takhrij of the Kashshaf: the correct form is al-Kalbiyya, with the lam sukun.

﴿or the male attendants (tabi'in)﴾, who serve for food or other purposes, [p. 263] ﴿who have no physical desire (ghayr uli al-irbah)﴾, i.e., who have no need for sexual enjoyment with women, ﴿among the men﴾, such as elderly men who are worn out, or those with an ailment that prevents their desire, and likewise one who has been castrated, according to the story of Mabur. ﴿or﴾ of ﴿the child﴾, i.e., of the kind of child, and a child (tifl) is a young one who has not reached puberty (ḥulm) or fifteen years of age. Originally it means tender and soft of anything, and it may be named so because it comes out mixed with the dirt the pregnant woman eats. Al-Qamus (the lexicon) says: "ṭafila al-nabt (the plant) like faraha, and ṭafula with a ḍamma, tatfīlan: the dust struck it. Al-ṭufāl, like ghurāb and saḥāb: dry clay." Al-Qazzaz said: "The people of Najd call it al-kalām, and the common folk say ṭifl for a type of it."

﴿who do not yet perceive the private matters of women (lam yaẓharū 'alā 'awrāt al-nisā')﴾, i.e., who have not yet attained the purposeful gaze for inspection, because they have not reached the age of desire for that.

Since He forbade display, He drew attention to a hidden matter within it, and said: ﴿And let them not strike their feet﴾, i.e., with their anklets and other adornments on them. Since this is for general announcement, He made the verb passive and said: ﴿so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾, i.e., by the covering they were commanded to wear, ﴿by the sound arising from the movement when striking as mentioned﴾. Included in this meaning is perfume, and the prohibition of this implies the prohibition against the place of it on the body by a fortiori reasoning.

When He, glory be to Him, finished what He commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to advance regarding men and women, and since it is known that the lowly servant, created with weakness, which necessitates shortcoming, will not be able to give the Exalted, Great Master His due, however much he strives and exerts himself, [p. 264] He followed it with gentleness, turning toward them in commanding them to turn toward Him, as an indication that the matter is extremely difficult, and that the human being, being a locus of error and shortcoming, however diligent he is, can only be met by the kindness of the Merciful, the Compassionate. So He said: ﴿And turn in repentance to Allah﴾, i.e., return to obedience to the Supreme King, whatever deviation occurs from you, as you used to do in the days of ignorance, ﴿all together﴾, your men and your women, ﴿O believers﴾. The expression by attribute indicates the high station of repentance: that only one firmly rooted in faith can sustain it, one who knows that, however much he strives, he falls short. This command is obligatory, and if it is for those firmly rooted in faith, then whoever is below them is a fortiori included. ﴿So that you may succeed﴾, i.e., that you may be hopeful of attaining the goal, which was mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Mu'minun as conditional upon those qualities, among them safeguarding trusts, especially regarding private parts.

Al-Ghazali said in the Book of Repentance of the Ihya' ('Ulum al-Din): The human being, insofar as he is created with deficiency, is never free of what necessitates repentance for him. If he is free at some times from sin of the limbs, he is not free from the intention of sins in the heart. If he is free of that, he is not free from the whispering of Satan by bringing in scattered thoughts that distract from the remembrance of Allah. If he is free of that, he is not free from heedlessness [p. 265] and deficiency in knowledge of Allah, His attributes, and His acts. All of this is deficiency, and it has causes, and abandoning its causes by occupying oneself with their opposites is a return from one path to its opposite. Repentance means return. It is not conceivable that a child of Adam is free of this deficiency; they differ only in degrees.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 32:

When He, glory be to Him, had set forth to His servants, in general terms, the matters concerning circumstances and persons regarding fornication (zina) and its causes, ruling, establishing, admonishing and warning, He followed it with the means of chastity (al-'ismah), which are an excellent aid to repentance. So He said, giving guidance: ﴿And marry off the unmarried (al-ayama) among you﴾. Al-ayama is a transposed form of ayayim, the plural of ayyim, on the pattern fa'il, from the root ama (its middle radical is a yaa'), and it means one who is without a spouse, whether male or female, virgin or not. ﴿Among you﴾ means among your free people. The word ayyim dispenses with mentioning righteousness, because it is not said of one who falls short of the rank of marriage. ﴿And the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾, that is, fit for marriage, ﴾, that is, your male and female slaves, out of precaution for their interests and to guard them from corruption, in compliance with what the hadith urged: "Marry, so that you may multiply, for I shall boast of you before the nations on the Day of Resurrection."

Since marriage entails a burden that deters people because of it, given the human disposition to panic at the scarcity of provision, He answered as if someone had said: a person may be unable because he is destitute, so He said: ﴿If they are poor﴾, that is, any of those mentioned, free or slave, and the use of the present tense indicates that in marriage there may be hardship and ease. ﴿Poor﴾ means in wealth. ﴿Allah will enrich them﴾, that is, He to whom all perfection belongs, once they marry ﴿out of His bounty﴾, because He has decreed for every soul its provision, so their poverty should not prevent you from marrying them off. From Ibn Abi Hatim, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Obey Allah in what He has commanded you regarding marriage, and He will fulfil for you what He has promised you of wealth.

Al-Baghawi said: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I am amazed at one who seeks wealth without marriage," and he recited this verse. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Seek wealth through marriage," and he recited this verse. (Narrated by Ibn Jarir.) Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, traced back to the Prophet: "Three are a right upon Allah to help them: the one who marries seeking chastity, the slave who seeks to purchase his freedom, and the one who fights in the way of Allah." This is supported by what is in the Sahih regarding the hadith of the woman who gave herself in marriage, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married her to a man who had not found anything, not even an iron ring.

Since the implied meaning is: then Allah is the Possessor of great bounty, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾, that is, the Possessor of majesty and honour. He is, by the vastness of His power, driving to the woman what He has decreed for her through the hand of the husband, and by the comprehensiveness of His knowledge He causes its means to come about.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 33:**

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded what protects from temptation, namely lowering the gaze, and then commanded what guards one's chastity through marriage, and encouraged them by promising wealth, though this promise concerned what comes after marriage, He placed His words about it first, to encourage a person toward reliance on Allah (tawakkul) and chastity (ihsan). Before this there were things that might prevent marriage, either the inability to find the bridal gift (mahr) and what must be paid before it, or the unwillingness of the servant or others to have his child be a slave or something else. So He followed it with His words, urging the suppression of the commanding self (nafs ammarah) when one is unable: ﴿And let those who cannot find a marriage keep themselves chaste﴾, that is, let them strive greatly to seek chastity and to attain it, away from what is unlawful, ﴿until Allah enriches them﴾, that is, Allah, who encompasses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿out of His bounty﴾, in that by which marriage was made impossible for them.

Since, as mentioned before, one of the obstacles is the fear of enslavement for the child of one who has high aspiration and a noble soul, when the child would be a slave, He followed this with His words: ﴿And those who seek the writing [of emancipation] from among those whom your right hands possess﴾, that is, those who seek it with firm determination. The "writing" (al-kitab) is the mukatabah (a contract of manumission by which a slave purchases his freedom in installments). Whether male or female, He used the word "what" (ma) to indicate the deficiency inherent in slavery. ﴿Then make a writing with them﴾, that is, it is recommended (nadban), because it is an exchange (mu'awadah) that includes kindness toward what they pay you in installments; when they have paid it, they are freed. ﴿If you know good in them﴾, that is, a sound disposition (tasarruf salih) in their religion and their worldly affairs, lest their condition deteriorate after they become independent. Ibn Kathir said: Abu Dawud related in Kitab al-Marasil from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you know a trade in them, and do not let them go to be a burden upon people." End of quote.

Perhaps He expressed "knowledge" where "assumption" is meant, for this reason. ﴿And give them﴾, which is obligatory when they have paid you, ﴿from the wealth of Allah﴾, that is, the wealth which has encompassed everything by His blessing, because He is the Great King, ﴿which He has given you﴾, even if by remitting part of the amount of the mukatabah.

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded generosity in the matter of slaves, sometimes with their persons and sometimes with wealth, He forbade what contradicts it, saying: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls﴾, that is, your female slaves. Perhaps He used the term "youth" (futuwwah) to stir them toward lofty character, and to shame them for seeking manliness from a female slave, ﴿to prostitution﴾, that is, fornication, so that you may take from them what they earn from that.

Since compulsion to fornication is not valid except when they desire chastity, and this is rare among slave girls, He said: ﴿if﴾ with the particle of doubt, ﴿they desire chastity﴾. In this there is an increase in the reprehensibility of compelling this act, since women in general avoid it out of chastity, though they are naturally inclined to love it. How much more so when no restraint of fear or shame prevents them, as with female slaves? How much more so when they are permitted it? How much more so when they are forced to it? He indicated with the form of the verb (tafa'ul) and by mentioning desire that this would not occur except from very great chastity. He increased the portrayal of reprehensibility by mentioning the reason for committing this shame in His words: ﴿that you may seek﴾, that is, seek earnestly, with strong desire, by compelling them to the vile act, ﴿the goods of the worldly life﴾, for the goods (ʿaraḍ) are subject to passing away, and "the world" (al-dunya) is derived from baseness (dana'ah).

When Allah, glorified is He, forbade compulsion, He encouraged the masters to repent if they had transgressed in it, saying: ﴿And whoever compels them﴾, without saying "if they are compelled," and He used the present tense to inform that He accepts repentance from one who transgressed after the revelation of the verse. He used the proper name in His words: ﴿then indeed Allah﴾, to inform that the Majestic is not without hope of mercy. Perhaps He used the expression "after" to indicate pardon for the inclination toward that act at the moment of committing it, if the aversion returns afterward, for the soul then cannot control its hatred of it. So He said: ﴿after their compulsion, is Forgiving﴾, that is, toward them and toward the masters, veiling that sin if they repent, ﴿Merciful﴾, by granting success to both categories toward what pleases Him.

And when Allah, glorified is He, had completed these verses concerning the innocence of ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, along with their preliminaries and conclusions, He said, joining by conjunction to His earlier words, ﴿And We have sent down in it clear signs, that you may remember﴾ [al-Nur: 1], ﴿And We have certainly sent down﴾, meaning by what We possess of greatness, as encouragement and warning for you, ﴿to you﴾, meaning so that you may take heed, ﴿clear signs﴾, in which the truth is distinguished from falsehood, made evident through transmitted text (naql) and reason (ʿaql), to such a degree that, because of the intensity of their clarity, they make clear to whoever reflects upon them the paths of rightness, just as We have made this clear to whoever reflects upon it concerning the innocence of ʿĀ'isha, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her, and what preceded it and followed it, of that which is your welfare in religion and in worldly life (p-271). ﴿And an example﴾, meaning and a likeness to your circumstances, ﴿from those who passed away before you﴾, meaning from their circumstances as revealed by Allah to them in the Torah (al-Tawrah), concerning situations of close association, unlawful intercourse (zina), and false accusation (qadhf) against the innocent, such as Yusuf and Maryam, peace be upon them both, and their exoneration. I have already mentioned much of this in Surat al-Ma'idah and elsewhere, and what has come to be, through the excellence of its arrangement in this book and the wondrous intricacy of its weaving, among those of understanding, like proverbs that circulate and orbits that revolve. ﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾, by what it contains of rulings and distinctions that disclose underlying causes, reminding of what brings one near to Allah, illuminating the heart, producing love and affection, and removing the burden in the breast.

[Page 272] Then he gave the reason for its descent, according to this most upright manner and firm arrangement, with His saying: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾. That is, He Whose power and knowledge encompass all things is the possessor of light (dhu nur) for the heavens and the earth, because He manifests them by bringing them into existence and bringing into existence their inhabitants, and He guides them by illuminating them with knowledge. This knowledge makes its possessor, through His guidance, to the straight path, like one walking in the light of the sun, who does not place anything in other than its proper place, just as one walking in the light does not place a foot anywhere other than where it is fitting. There is no doubt that light is that by which things appear and are revealed. So He, glorified be He, is the One who manifests them, and they, and what is in them, are indications of His manifestation, and that He is perfect in power, all-encompassing in knowledge, possessing all attributes of perfection, and free from any defect. At the end of Surat ash-Shura there is something very beneficial here.

Since it is impossible that anyone among the inhabitants of the two horizons (the east and the west) should be lost from a light that fills the two horizons, He explained the reason for its concealment despite the manifestness of its radiance, its breadth, and the strength of its beam, such that most people went astray from it. So he said, clarifying by attributing the light to His pronoun, that reporting about Him as light is a metaphor and not a literal fact, alerting that His guiding signs shine through the doubts that arise from the prevailing illusions among creation, which are like darknesses: ﴿the likeness of His light﴾, that is, of the light by which He guided to the way of right guidance, despite its being hidden from some people while being intensely manifest. It is His signs that point to Him, from His sayings and His actions. ﴿Is like a niche (mishkah)﴾, that is, like a recess (kuwwah), meaning a hole that is not a through-passage, in a wall. Al-Baghawi said: If it has an opening through which it passes, then it is a kuwwah.

Since he placed the niche in this parable in an obscure way, he put it first to create anticipation for its explanation, and then followed it with his saying, explaining it: ﴿Within it is a lamp (misbah)﴾, that is, a large, piercing lamp. [Page 273] It is a large wick, that is, a large burning wick, from the word sabah, which is the light of dawn, and the misbah, which is the great star. Al-Baghawi said: Its origin is light (ḍaw').

When the lamp is in the niche, its rays gather together, so it becomes more brilliant. If it were in an open space, its rays would disperse. Then he brought the rest of the statement as a new sentence, in anticipation of a question, to magnify it, so he said: ﴿The lamp is in a glass (zujajah)﴾, that is, a lantern.

Since there is glass that is at the extreme of clarity, he explained that this one is of that kind, so he said: ﴿The glass is as if it were﴾, that is, in intense clarity, ﴿a star (kawkab)﴾. He compared it to a star and not to the sun or moon, because eclipses affect them. ﴿Shining (durri)﴾, that is, sparkling with lights. When it is in a clear glass, the rays separating from it are reflected from some sides of the glass to others, because of its clarity and transparency, and so the light increases and reaches its limit. Just as the sun's ray, when it falls on water or clear glass, the light multiplies until the like of that light appears in what faces it. Al-Zajjaj said: durri is derived from "dara'a," meaning to move forward swiftly, so its light is multiplied. [Page 274] Since among lamps there are also those whose light is weak, he explained that this one is not like that, so he said: ﴿Kindled﴾, that is, the lamp is lit, by its flame being intensified. Since this light varies according to what burns in it, if it is pure and unmixed oil, it is intense. The oils that are burned, among which there is none that shows clarity like olive oil, because it may reach in clarity and fineness the level of water, with added whiteness and a light that moves through its parts. He said: ﴿From a blessed tree﴾, that is, its oil, ﴿blessed (mubarakah)﴾, that is, abundant in permanence and goodness, whose place of growth is good, ﴿an olive tree (zaytunah)﴾.

Since oil varies according to its tree in terms of whether it is screened from the sun or exposed to it, because a tree may weaken and its fruit may become bad when something stands between it and the sun, he explained that this tree is not like that, so he said: ﴿Neither eastern (sharqiyyah)﴾, that is, it is not related to the east alone, because it is situated where the sun reaches it only at sunrise, [Page 275] but it is in the shelter of a mountain that shades it when the sun is about to set. ﴿Nor western (gharbiyyah)﴾, because it is on the slope of a mountain that shields it from the sun at sunrise. Rather, it is exposed to the sun from the time of sunrise until the time of sunset, so that its fruit is more ripened and its oil is purer. Al-Baghawi said: This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in the narration of 'Ikrimah, al-Kalbi and most of the scholars.

So it is because of the purity of its essence, the cleanness of its place of growth, and its exposure to the sun and the winds, such that ﴿its oil nearly glows even if no fire touched it﴾, because of its intense clarity.

Since he knew from this that this parable has lights that support one another through the assistance of the niche, the glass, the lamp and the oil, nothing remains that strengthens its light, increases its brightness, and supplies it with pure illumination. He said, concerning the thing parabled: ﴿Light upon light﴾, that is, the divine knowledge is of great breadth: whenever the gaze roams within it and the reins of thought are released, it brings forth wonders, and it cannot be brought to a limit.

Since the report about the multiplication of this light would necessitate the belief that it is hidden from no one, He indicated that, by the all-encompassing nature of His knowledge and the completeness of His power, whoever He wills goes blind to it despite its intense radiance and great brilliance. So he said: ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾, that is, [Page 276] by His greatness that encompasses everything, just as Allah guided those among the believers who were guided to clear 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, before the revelation of her innocence.

By Allah's choosing her for His Prophet ﷺ, for He chooses for him none but the good and pure, and similar things. It is known that the counterpart of this is ﴿And Allah leaves astray whom He wills from His light﴾. And it is known that the reason most people went astray from it is only that the Capable One has veiled it by a defect in the perception of whoever He, glorified be He, wills to lead astray, not because of a defect in the light, as the poet said:

The star is made small in the eyes' sight, its form,
So the fault lies in the eye's sight, not in the star's smallness.

As will come explanation of this at His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan: 45]. And what passed a moment ago in the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the souls, is beneficial here.

Since it is as if it were said: Allah struck this parable for you so that you would reflect upon it and benefit from it, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And Allah strikes the parables for people﴾, that is, by what He has of encompassing complete power and all-encompassing knowledge, [Page 277] knowing them, to bring them near to understanding, ﴿perhaps they will be guided﴾. ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, He to Whom belongs all attributes of perfection, ﴿is Knowing of all things﴾, that is, of these and of others. He explains everything in a way that eases its path. So trust what He says, and if you do not understand it, then blame yourselves and examine it closely, and He, glorified be He, will open to you what has been closed of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 36:

Since it was as if it had been said: "What will this niche (mishkah) be?", he said, providing an answer to this question: ﴿In houses﴾, meaning in the walls of houses. He used the plural to indicate that what is meant by "niche" is a category and not a single one. In the unity of the houses and the unity of the instruments of light there is an indication of His great might. ﴿God has permitted﴾, meaning He empowered by His majesty, so He permitted, recommended and obligated. ﴿That they be raised﴾, physically in construction, and figuratively by dedicating them to righteous deeds, by every one who raises them whom He, glorified is He, has permitted to do so. So when a person enters them, he should seek protection from the enemy by what Abu Dawud related from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say, when he entered the mosque: 'I seek refuge in Allah the Mighty, and in His noble face, and in His eternal authority, from the accursed Satan.' ʿUqbah ibn Muslim said: When he says that, Satan says: 'He has been protected from me for the rest of the day.'"

﴿And that His name be mentioned therein﴾, by every mentioner whom He, glorified is He, has permitted. ﴿Glorified therein﴾, meaning with remembrance pure of any impurity and sincere of any deceit. ﴿by Him﴾, meaning specifically for Him. ﴿in the mornings﴾, meaning the early hours (al-ibkar), with the dawn prayer. ﴿and the evenings﴾, meaning the afternoons (al-ashal), with the remaining prayers, so that they begin their deeds and conclude them with His remembrance, that they may be protected in between and that blessing may be granted to them in what they engage in. The word "al-asil" is in the plural because it is certain that what is meant is the noon, afternoon, sunset and night prayers. Al-Baghawi said: because the term "al-asil" comprises them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 37:

﴿Men﴾, i.e., men ﴿whom neither trade nor sale distracts﴾, i.e., by selling, buying, or other than these, through which a profit appears to them.

Since a person may be compelled to part by sale with some of what he owns, in order to sustain himself with its price or to reach with it some necessary matters to which he has no access except by it, or to obtain what he does not own in the same way, and since selling in trade is also the principal aim, because it is the place where the profit that cannot be given up is realized, He said: ﴿nor sale﴾, i.e., even if it is not in the manner of trade. The word "bay'" (sale) is used in common for the acquisition, which is purchase (shira'), and for the disposal. ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾, i.e., He who possesses majesty and honour absolutely, through prayer and other than it. So they are [ﾠ](p-279) at every time in witnessing and vigilance toward the One who made Himself known to them by the attributes of perfection. And that does not distract them from ﴿establishing prayer﴾, which is the purification of spirits. He repeated it after mentioning it by "glorification," explicitly naming it, emphasizing it, and urging the guarding of its time, because that is among its constituents, and likewise all its limits, even in the briefest form that is the least of perfection. This is indicated by the omission of the ta' (in the word for prayer, meaning the word is written without the feminine ending), signalling that this praise does not depend on the highest degree of perfection. Nor from ﴿giving zakat﴾, which is the growth and increase of bodies (the literal meaning of zakah). He specified men, although the attendance of women at the mosques is a well-known sunnah, to indicate that their prayer in their homes is more excellent, because of what Abu Dawud related in his Sunan (a collection of hadith arranged by legal topics) and Ibn Khuzaymah in his Sahih (a collection of authentic hadith) from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "A woman's prayer in her house is better than her prayer in her courtyard, and her prayer in her inner chamber is better than her prayer in her house." The makhda' is the storeroom. Also, Imam Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Khuzaymah, and al-Hakim related from Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best mosques for women are the innermost parts of their houses." And Ahmad, Ibn Khuzaymah, and Ibn Hibban in their Sahihs related from Umm Humayd, the wife of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi, [ﾠ](p-280) may Allah be pleased with both of them, that she said: "O Messenger of Allah! I love to pray with you." He said: "I know that you love to pray with me, but your prayer in your house is better than your prayer in your inner chamber, and your prayer in your inner chamber is better than your prayer in your courtyard, and your prayer in your courtyard is better than your prayer in your people's mosque, and your prayer in your people's mosque is better than your prayer in my mosque." She said: So she gave an order, and a mosque was built for her at the furthest and darkest part of her house, and she used to pray in it until she met Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

When He described the men mentioned with what He described them with, He mentioned the reason for their doing so, to add to their praise, and said: ﴿They fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be turned over﴾, and it is the Day of Resurrection, [a day] on which ﴿hearts and eyes will be turned over﴾, i.e., because of the intensity of its terror, a visible turning over, which is indicated by the affirmation of the two ta's (in the verb, indicating the feminine plural form). This is between hope for salvation and fear of destruction. It may be said (and Allah knows best) that the niches are the mosques, the glass is the men, and the lamps are the hearts, and their brilliance is what they contain of meanings that move them to remembrance. The described tree [ﾠ](p-281) is the likeness of bodies, which Allah has purified from defilements and disposed to uprightness. The oil is a likeness of the beautiful secrets that He, glory be to Him, placed in them. It has been reported in some traditions that the mosques for the people of the heavens are like the stars for the people of the earth. In al-Tabarani's Mu'jam al-Awsat (a dictionary-style arrangement of hadith) from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "like a niche," he said: "the inside of Muhammad (ﷺ)"; "the glass" is his heart; "the lamp" is the light in his heart; "the tree" is Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿neither of the East nor of the West﴾ [al-Nur: 35]: neither Jewish nor Christian.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 38:

When Allah, exalted is He, had explained the deeds of these men by which they turned towards Him and turned away from all else, He explained their ultimate aim in them, saying: ﴿That He may reward them﴾, meaning, they do that so that Allah may reward them ﴿Allah﴾, meaning in the abode of His honour after the Resurrection, with His greatness, majesty, generosity and beauty ﴿the best of what they did﴾, meaning, their recompense. And He will forgive them their misdeeds ﴿and increase them of His bounty﴾, meaning, beyond the justice of recompense, with what they did not deserve, as is the custom of the generous.

Since the sense is: Allah, by virtue of His majesty, greatness and perfection, does not consent to limit the reward of the one who does good to what he deserves alone, He follows this with an explanation, because His power and greatness have no limit, with His saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning (p. 282) the One who has no equal, so there is no objection to Him, ﴿gives provision to whom He wills﴾. Since the meaning is provision that exceeds all measure and cannot be counted, He expressed it with His saying: ﴿without reckoning﴾. This is a *kināya* (metonymy, an expression that signifies a meaning indirectly) for abundance. It is also possible that along with abundance there is success (*tawfīq*), so that it is glad tidings of the absence of reckoning in the Hereafter as well, entirely and altogether, because that person who was provided for did not do anything that would incur a liability upon him, so he is not called to account; or he is called to account but not punished. Thus the intended meaning of the negation of reckoning is the negation of its hardship and punishment. It is also possible that the provision is increased beyond sufficiency. And it has been reported that there is no reckoning in it. Ibn Kathir narrated from Ibn Abi Hatim, with his chain, from Asma' bint Yazid (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah gathers the first and the last on the Day of Resurrection, a caller will call out with a voice that the creatures can hear: 'The people of the gathering will know who is most deserving of honour. Let those stand whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah.' Then they will stand, and they will be few. Then all the rest of creation will be called to account."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 39:

When God, exalted is He, informed that those who followed the Light of the Truth, glory be to Him, and who reached—by means of His reward, because of what the Light guided them to of righteous deeds—realities which are, in the matter itself, the realities, He then informed about their opposites, those who followed falsehood, whose rugged, towering mountains stood between the sight of their insights and those Lights, in contrast to their state. So He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., who concealed, by what they had adhered to of misguidance, what had spread of the Light of God. ﴿Their deeds﴾ existing on the Day of Recompense ﴿are like a mirage﴾, which is what one sees at midday in the deserts, clinging to the ground, glittering as if it were water; and whenever you draw near to it, it recedes until you reach a mountain or the like, and then it vanishes. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': the mirage is a ray of light that uncovers itself, so it flows and runs like water, as an illusion. Ibn Kathir said: it is seen from a distance as if it were a full sea, and that occurs only after midday; as for al-Al (the mirage of the morning), it occurs at the beginning of the day, appearing as if it were water between the sky and the earth—end of quote. Al-Baghawi said: al-Al is what rises above the earth, and it is a ray seen between the sky and the earth in the early mornings, resembling a sheet, in which figures are raised; the small appears large in it, and the short appears tall. Al-Raqraq occurs in the evenings, and it is what shimmers from the mirage, i.e., it comes and goes.

﴿In a valley (bi-qi'ah)﴾ is the plural of qa', which is level, low-lying ground from which the mountains and hillocks have receded—so said al-Qamus. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qazzaz said in his Diwan: qi'ah and qa' are one and the same, and both are the flat, smooth land in which dust gathers. Al-Farra': qi'ah is the plural of qa' like jar and jirah. Al-Saghani said in Majma' al-Bahrayn: al-qa' is the level part of the land; its plurals are aqwa', aquw', and qi'an; the waw became ya' because of the kasrah before it; qi'ah is like qa', and it is also from the waw; some say it is a plural. Ibn Jarir said: al-qa' is what is spread out and wide in the land, and in it the mirage occurs. 'Abd al-Ghafir al-Farisi said in Majma' al-Gharaib: al-Farra' said: al-qa' is a pool of water; and al-qa' is a wide level place in a depression of the land, over which rain collects and holds, and its vegetation becomes even; its plural is qi'ah and qi'an.

﴿The thirsty one thinks it to be water﴾, i.e., the one who is severely parched from weakness of mind, ﴿so he heads for it and keeps on going﴾; ﴿until, when he reaches it﴾, i.e., reaches the place he imagined, ﴿he finds it to be nothing﴾ of anything, so his aim gains him nothing but increased thirst with increased fatigue and distance from places of hope; so his distress intensifies, his resources are cut off, and he perishes. (p-285) Likewise the disbeliever thinks his deeds will benefit him in something, but when they come, they have destroyed him.

Since God encompasses everything by His knowledge and power in every place, He said: ﴿And he finds God with him﴾, i.e., the power of Him who encompasses all things, ﴿with him﴾, i.e., with that place which he aimed at, when he imagined good in it, and his hope failed; ﴿so He pays him his account in full﴾, i.e., the recompense of his deeds according to what his deeds require by the judgment of justice. This ignorant one was not satisfied with the disappointment and grief that he did not find what he aimed at as nothing, like others with the mirage, until he found there the angels of punishment dragging him toward a fire whose captive is not released and whose blaze is not extinguished.

Since He, glory be to Him, has no need of a scribe, no confusion enters upon Him, it is not difficult for Him to record anything however much it is, and no one can escape what He wills for him by any kind of trick, He expressed this by His saying: ﴿And God﴾, i.e., He to whom belongs complete power and comprehensive knowledge, ﴿is swift at reckoning﴾, i.e., because He has no need of retention in a heart, nor of counting on fingers, nor of anything other than that; rather, He knows all of that before the servant does it and after he has done it. Nothing of it or of anything else escapes Him.

[p-286] When Allah, glory be to Him, had shown through this example that they reach nothing but exhaustion, which leads to ruin, and since no sane person would do this to himself, He struck another example, between what drives them to fall into the calamity of the first (namely, walking without a guide), which casts one into *khabṭ al-ʿashwāʾ* (blundering about blindly in the dark), and one who walks in darkness. He said, conjoining with ﴿like a mirage﴾ [al-Nur: 39], His words: ﴿or﴾, for choice. That is, their deeds, because they have no benefit, are like a mirage, and because they are empty of the light of truth, they are ﴿like darknesses﴾. Or it is for variety: if their outward appearance is good, they are like the mirage, and if they are ugly, they are like the darknesses. Or it is for division by considering two times: like darknesses in this world and like the mirage in the Hereafter. ﴿In a sea﴾ is the example of the heart of the disbeliever, ﴿deep﴾, that is, possessing *lujj* (the deep, churning depth), which is *al-lujj* itself, indicating that it is profound, with no reachable bottom, because *al-lujj* is the greatest part of the water. It may also be the plural of *lujjah*. The most fitting reading here is that it is attributed to the plural, because it is more terrifying, and the context calls for terror. Al-Qazzaz said in his *Diwan*: "The *lujjah* of the sea is well known, and it is the place from which you see no land or mountain. A *baḥr lujjī* is a sea of wide depth. The plural of *lujjah* is *lujaj* and *lajj*."

﴿Covered by a wave﴾, that is, it covers this sea and rises over it, or it reaches the one within it. ﴿A wave﴾, and this is like what covers his heart of ignorance, doubt and bewilderment, which is present ﴿above it﴾, that is, this wave, ﴿a wave﴾ another ﴿above it﴾, that is, this second wave piled upon the first, ﴿clouds﴾ that have veiled the stars. This is the example of *al-rayn* (the rust or veil), the sealing and the stamping upon the heart, so that no sky is seen and no earth.

[p-287] Since this is a fearsome matter, He pointed to its terror and portrayal with His words: ﴿darknesses﴾, that is, of the sea, the two waves and the clouds, ﴿one above another﴾. Since the intended meaning is the total encompassing of the direction, He did not state the preposition, but said: ﴿one above another﴾, piled up. For this reason it is extremely remote that any sight could penetrate them. Hence He said: ﴿if he brings out his hand﴾, that is, the one within this sea, as indicated by the meaning though he has not been mentioned, ﴿his hand﴾, which is the nearest thing to him, ﴿he can hardly see it﴾, that is, the one within it can hardly approach seeing it, let alone it being visible, because Allah has concealed from him every light by these dense darknesses. This is an example of his deed, and that it is a nonexistence, in accordance with what has preceded, that all nonexistence is darkness. So he has no deed that could become anything, and he does not come near to that, because he has no capacity whatsoever. ﴿And whoever Allah does not give﴾, that is, the King, the Greatest, ﴿light﴾ from among the lights, which is the power of bringing into existence and manifesting, ﴿for him there is no light﴾ at all, because He, glory be to Him, conceals His light, even though it fills the heavens and the earth, from whomever He wills, by veils of the atmospheres, for He is capable of what He wills.

[p. 288] Since the subsistence of all affairs, and their manifestation in every way, depends only on light, physically through bringing into existence and figuratively through making existent things into visible signs that point to their Originator, God said, indicating what He had told us, that He alone is the Light of the heavens and the earth, that is, the One who brings them into being by His knowledge and power, and that whoever He clothes with His light, then on the Day of Resurrection, when He will recompense creation according to what knowledge requires (which is light in reality) of the measures of their deeds, and whoever He strips of the light perishes:

﴿Do you not see﴾, that is, do you not know, O head of those who attain the rank of ihsan (excellence), knowledge that is as firm as direct witnessing, ﴿that God﴾, who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿is glorified by﴾, that is, is exalted above every trace of deficiency, for His sake alone, by what He has of complete power in it, ﴿whoever is in the heavens﴾

Since the structure of the surah is based on the all-encompassing scope of knowledge and power, He did not emphasize, but said: ﴿and the earth﴾, that is, both of them and everything in them, by the tongue of their state or by the instrument of their speech. He indicated that the intended meaning is generality by conjoining what does not reason, and He expressed it with "whoever" (man) because the one who is glorifying is among the functions of rational beings.

Since the sign of the birds is more indicative, because it is more wondrous, He specified them, saying: ﴿and the birds, spreading their wings﴾, that is, extending their wings in the air of the sky. There is no doubt that none holds them up except God, and His holding them in the air, although they are heavy bodies, and His determining for them in it the contraction and extension, is a decisive proof of the perfection of His power.

[p. 289] Since knowledge is attributed to that which is a cause, such as a written book and the like, and an active participle is derived for a thing from what it is associated with, as one says, "its night is standing (in prayer), and its day is fasting," (as in the verse) ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], and since the traces of power were inscribed well upon every existing thing, and very clear on the surfaces of everything, the created beings thereby pointed to their Creator and to every attribute of perfection He has, so it is valid to apply knowledge to them and to ascribe it to them. Thus He said: ﴿Each﴾, that is, of the created beings, ﴿has known﴾, that is, by that which was the cause of its knowledge, from the signs in it that indicate and make known what its Originator has of attributes of perfection, ﴿its prayer﴾, that is, the way by which it connects with its Master and is related to Him, ﴿and its glorification﴾, that is, the state by which its Maker is cleared of blemish and exalted above deficiency. Their states have spoken clearly of this, standing in place of the explanation of their speech. This one by its standing, silent and still; this one by its growing, swaying and rising; compelled and subdued. This one by its movement through will, and aiming at the aspects of its benefits and distancing from the states of its harms, by mere natural disposition and what was deposited in its nature. This one by its speech and reason, its intelligence and excellence. Yet the relation of each of them to earth and heaven is one and the same. What clearly indicates this is what Imam Ahmad narrated in the Musnad from Abdullah ibn Amr, may God be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ:

"Noah, peace be upon him, instructed his son at his death: 'La ilaha illa Allah (there is no god but God). For if the seven heavens and the seven earths were placed in a balance, they would be outweighed by it. And Subhan Allah wa bihamdih (Glory be to God and praise be to Him), for it is the prayer of every thing, and by it creation is provided for.'"

[p. 290] Al-Ghazali said in the Ihya': It was narrated that a man came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "The world has turned away from me and my means have become scant." The Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "Where are you from the prayer of the angels and the glorification of creatures, by which they are provided for?" He said: I said, "And what is it, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Subhan Allah wa bihamdih, Subhan Allah al-'Azim, astaghfir Allah (I seek God's forgiveness) one hundred times, between the rising of dawn and your praying the morning prayer. The world will come to you humbled and abased. And God will create from every word an angel who glorifies God until the Day of Resurrection, and its reward is yours."

The Hafiz Zayn al-Din al-Iraqi said: It was narrated by al-Mustaghfiri in al-Da'awat from Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, and he said: "Strange, from the hadith of Malik, and I know of no origin for it from the hadith of Malik."

Since the implication is: then God is capable over all those affairs, He conjoined to it His saying: ﴿And God﴾, that is, the One who encompasses in knowledge and power, ﴿is Knowing of what they do﴾, by what has been established of what He informed you of in this surah, the subtleties of your sayings and states, your inner thoughts and your deeds. What has preceded in al-A'raf at His saying ﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185] is useful here.

(p-291) When he had informed of what is in the two worlds by that which entails dominion, in the most complete of its aspects, which entails the power to resurrect, he then informed of both of them explicitly, saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, the One besides whom there is no sovereign, ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, together with His being the owner, the subjugator, and the director of all that. So He combines possession (al-milk) and sovereignty (al-mulk).

Since the implied sense is: "And from Allah is the origin of all things through bringing them into existence from non-existence," He followed it with His saying: ﴿And to Allah is the destination﴾, that is, the One who has encompassing knowledge of everything, ﴿the destination﴾, meaning the return of all of them after annihilation. This implied element was omitted only because there is no disagreement about it.

Then He mentioned what is even more indicative of (divine) choice, saying, as a restatement of what preceded with an addition: ﴿God alternates the night and the day﴾, meaning He to whom all command belongs, by transforming darkness into light and light into darkness, and by diminution at one time and increase at another, with rain at one time and clear skies at another, ﴿the night and the day﴾. From that alternation there arises, from heat and cold, growth and ripening, and dryness, what dazzles the intellects. Therefore He said, drawing attention to the outcome: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, meaning the great matter mentioned from all that has preceded, ﴿is surely a lesson for those endowed with sight﴾, meaning those with penetrating insight and discerning hearts, through which they pass over to knowledge of what the Manager of that possesses of complete power and all-encompassing knowledge, which decisively indicates His oneness (tawhid).

When he first mentioned the conditions of the two horizons as evidence of His oneness, and singled out from them the heavenly effects, mentioning what waters the earth while omitting what plants grow from it because it is known, he then mentioned the conditions of the living creatures that come into being through it, as clear evidence of resurrection and a compelling proof against those who deny it. He said: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One who has complete knowledge and all-encompassing power, ﴿created every creature﴾, that is, of those things previously said to glorify Him.

When he mentioned kinds of animals, he used the indefinite form, unlike what occurs in al-Anbiya', and said: ﴿from water﴾, that is, gushing water, which is the greatest part of their substance, just as He created plants from ﴿hamir﴾ water in the same way. He made differences among them although all are from the same gushing water (p-294) in which there is no difference. ﴿So among them﴾, that is, among the creatures,

and since this is in the context of glorification, and He had given every soul the perception by which it knows its benefits and harms, He expressed the whole by the particle used for one who has reason, although they differ in discernment, and said: ﴿those who walk on their bellies﴾, that is, without legs. He placed this first because it is more indicative of power, and He called it walking by way of metaphor (istiʿarah) and congruence (mushakalah). ﴿And among them are those who walk on two legs﴾, that is, only two. ﴿And among them are those who walk on four﴾, that is, of hands and feet. In this there is an alert to whoever walks on more than that, and to it points His saying: ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾. He used the Name of Majesty to inform of the utmost greatness, and said ﴿what He wills﴾ to show that He did it by His power and choice, with no entry for anything other than that in it, except by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

Since these proofs look most thoroughly toward the resurrection, and they were deniers of it, He emphasized His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom absolute perfection belongs, ﴿over all things﴾ of that and other than it ﴿is Competent﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 46:

Now that what Allah, exalted is He, possesses of attributes of perfection and of being free from every trace of deficiency has become clear by this, and the proofs of His oneness have stood firm upon their leg, and the demonstrations of His divinity have aligned in the most perfect alignment, He said, translating those proofs: ﴿Indeed We have sent down﴾, i.e., in this surah and what precedes it, by the greatness that is Ours, ﴿verses﴾, i.e., of wisdoms, rulings, proofs and parables, ﴿clear﴾, there being no obscurity in any of them for anyone among creation, because Allah has willed your guidance, some of you through explanation and some of you through the creation of submission ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King, ﴿guides whom He wills﴾ from among all the servants ﴿to a straight path﴾, by potential through the sending down of the verses, and by actual act through the creation of faith and humble submission, so that they believe with a firm faith.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 24, verse 47:

Since the concealment of these verses from some after their clarification is more remarkable than the initial setting forth of them, the context clearly indicates that the implied meaning is: "And God misguides whom He wills, so they disbelieve in the signs and the wise Reminder."
